So the split is degree, not direction. overrides.rationale: The behavior target converges to exactly one: the django.db.backends DEBUG record emitted by CursorDebugWrapper.debug_sql must carry the connection alias. Choosing that placement and key name is a Django house-style call, hence P1 with U5 rather than P0.

resolution_notes: Both passes target the same change -- put the connection alias into the django.db.backends debug logging done by CursorDebugWrapper.debug_sql -- so the split is only P0 vs P1. On the one contested fact, r1 is right and r2 is wrong: r2's rationale says 'the linked pull request is only a bare URL in this packet and contributes nothing', but category_status shows linked_artifacts materialized (direct_link_cutoff_verified) and dumping linked:django/django#11994 yields real text, the PR title 'Fixed #30934 - Include database alias in django.db.backends debug output' plus 'This is useful if you're working with database routers and want to inspect where SQL statements are being routed to'. That is why I keep r1 as base -- its evidence list and provenance correctly include the linked artifact. But the artifact only restates intent; it carries no sample output, and I confirmed no visible test pins the message either (tests/backends/tests.py test_debug_sql at 62-66 reads connection.queries, never the log record, and the file has no assertLogs on this logger). docs/ref/logging.txt 176-180 enumerates the extra context as duration, sql, params, which shows the structured surface is a documented named set but leaves the new key's name and the alias's position in the '(%.3f) %s; args=%s' message open. Target clear, exact surface resting on a house-style choice is the P1 definition, so I override r1 to P1/U5 with clarification_target convention; r1's predicted_direction, filled template and empty candidate_directions already satisfy the P1 shape, so no other fields change. r2 reached the same label but on a rationale that misdescribes the packet.

Both passes describe the same target -- stop the natural-key dependency sort from aborting serialization on circular references, skipping the sort where natural foreign keys cannot appear and making the remaining path best-effort. The split is whether the acceptance surface is pinned, and two checks against the frozen evidence say it is not. First, the reporter himself leaves an explicit unresolved design question in the issue body: 'sort_dependencies could be modified to allow loops unconditionally, or we could add an argument and default to disallowing loops in case any code outside of django is using this function?'. r1 dismisses this as 'internal API shape with no observable-behavior difference', but that does not survive the evidence -- sort_dependencies is a module-level name in django/core/serializers/__init__.py (159, signature sort_dependencies(app_list)) and the visible tests call it directly on that signature: tests/fixtures_regress/tests.py test_dependency_sorting through test_dependency_sorting_4 at 616-652 invoke serializers.sort_dependencies([('fixtures_regress', [...])]) and assert the returned model order. So whether third-party and existing callers keep getting the 'Can't resolve dependencies' exception is a real, externally visible consequence, and the reporter defers that call to maintainers -- U5, clarification_target convention. Second, r1's claim that the reporter's three call sites are 'all confirmed present in the retrieved code' is false. Grepping every retrieved file for sort_dependencies returns exactly one call, dumpdata.py:147 inside get_objects(); django/db/backends/base/creation.py is retrieved untruncated ([[1,302]]) and its serialize_db_to_string at 94-122 already builds get_objects() by iterating apps.get_app_configs() and calls serializers.serialize('json', get_objects(), indent=None, stream=out) with no sorting at all. The issue's third prescription is therefore stale against base_commit. That does not fork the behavior target -- that path already serializes in arbitrary order, so the prescription is a no-op there -- but it is one more reason the packet does not pin the surface the way P0 requires. r2 is base with no overrides: it is already P1/U5, and unlike r1 its rationale confines its code claims to what is actually there ('serializers/__init__.py lines 200-226 and dumpdata.py line 147 confirm the promotion loop and its caller').

missing_repository_evidence: DataArray._inplace_binary_op in xarray/core/dataarray.py: the traceback frame (line 2619 in the reporter's installed copy) falls in a gap between the retrieved slices [2363,2523] and [2671,2831], and grepping the retrieved dataarray.py for _inplace_binary_op returns no hit, so the frame that opens the _merge_inplace context manager is not in the packet
overrides.rationale: The report contrasts a working A + B against a failing A += B on the very same pair, which fixes what the result should be for the reported input, and xarray/core/coordinates.py 129-144 plus xarray/core/merge.py 203-214 expose the deliberately unaligned merge whose index equality check raises. What keeps this off P0 is that the packet also documents the current behavior as intentional and does not say how far the reconciliation should reach. The _merge_inplace body carries the comment 'don't include indexes in prioritized, because we didn't align first and we want indexes to be checked' (135-136), and doc/computation.rst 524-529 states as a design note: 'There is no automatic alignment between arguments when performing in-place arithmetic operations such as ``+=``. You will need to use manual alignment. This ensures in-place arithmetic never needs to modify data types.' So the fix cannot simply be general alignment of the right operand; it has to be scoped to the case the reporter hit, where the label sets are identical and only the order differs, so neither shape nor dtype changes. Where exactly that boundary sits -- partly overlapping indexes, where an in-place operation cannot resize the left operand -- is left open by the packet, and the DataArray frame that would show the current contract is truncated out. Bounded assumption, single behavior target: P1 with U2.

resolution_notes: Both passes give the same behavior target -- make A += B on DataArrays whose shared index holds the same labels in a different order complete with the result A = A + B already produces, instead of MergeError 'conflicting values for index'. The decisive evidence is one neither pass cited: doc/computation.rst 524-529 documents the present behavior as deliberate ('There is no automatic alignment between arguments when performing in-place arithmetic operations such as ``+=``... This ensures in-place arithmetic never needs to modify data types'), matching the in-code comment at coordinates.py 135-136 ('we didn't align first and we want indexes to be checked'). That kills r1's P0: the packet does not pin an acceptance surface, it documents a contract that a naive align-the-RHS fix would contradict, so the patch has to be scoped to the reorder-only case, and the packet never says what a partial overlap should do. That is precisely r2's U2, so r2's label stands and I keep it as base. I did override two things on r2. Its missing_repository_evidence claimed 'the packet's copy stops at line 1897', which is wrong -- the index shows dataarray.py slices running to [3519,3679]; the real situation is that the traceback frame falls in the gap between [2363,2523] and [2671,2831], and grepping the retrieved dataarray.py for _inplace_binary_op returns nothing, so r1's phrasing of that point was the accurate one. And I added docs to the evidence lists with doc/computation.rst provenance, plus a rationale that carries the doc note, so the merged record rests on the evidence that actually decided it.

Both passes land on the same spot and the same core outcome: guard the rewrite at sympy/core/power.py 373-374 so sqrt(1/tan(1 + I)) is constructed instead of blowing the stack. I confirmed the shared factual claim -- power.py is retrieved untruncated ([[1,1752]]) and the branch is exactly where both say, inside `if e.is_extended_real:` / `if e == -1:` / `if _half(other):`, with `if b.is_extended_real is False: return Pow(b.conjugate()/Abs(b)**2, other)` at 373-374, self-feeding because the rewritten quotient re-enters Pow.__new__ with the same half exponent. (The traceback in the issue body prints this as line 375, one off from the base_commit copy, but the reporter's own permalink is to L373-L374, so the target line is unambiguous.) What separates the two is whether the acceptance surface is pinned, and it is not. The issue supplies a reproduction and a traceback but its entire statement of the fix is 'There should be an additional check on this line' -- it never says which check, and it never says what the expression should come back as. Nothing else in the packet supplies it: there is no test_power.py among the eight visible_tests items (they are test_pickling, diagnose_imports, test_code_quality, test_expr, test_args, test_latex, test_theanocode, test_plot), linked_artifacts is unavailable (cutoff_unverifiable) and public_comments_until_cutoff is unavailable, so no maintainer discussion fixes the predicate either. Different admissible guards all terminate but return different symbolic forms -- an unevaluated sqrt(1/tan(1 + I)) versus a conjugate-over-Abs-squared form -- which is one behavior target with an unspecified surface, i.e. P1 with U2, not the two distinct targets that would make it P2. r1's 'the precise guard condition is implementation detail, not a behavior ambiguity' understates that the returned expression is itself observable. r2 is base with no overrides: it already carries P1/U2 with clarification_target expected_behavior and its rationale states the split correctly, that 'terminates rather than recursing' is settled while the predicate is not.

Both passes land on the same behavior target (Nominal axes adopt the categorical drawing convention: +/-0.5 limits with no margin, grid off, y inverted) and both cite the same sites; r2's code claims verify exactly -- Plotter._finalize_figure is at seaborn/_core/plot.py line 1628 and the string-limit +/-0.5 padding it generalises is at plot.py lines 1641-1644, and Nominal._setup is at seaborn/_core/scales.py line 149. The blocker axis is decided by a line neither pass cited: seaborn/categorical.py lines 198-204 already implements all three enumerated behaviors for the classic categorical plots -- 'ax.xaxis.grid(False); ax.set_xlim(-.5, n - .5, auto=None)' and 'ax.yaxis.grid(False); ax.set_ylim(n - .5, -.5, auto=None)'. That is unconditional grid suppression with no theme deference, and it is in the retrieved code. r2's U5 rests on the claim that the grid-versus-theme precedence rule 'is a project convention rather than something derivable from the files'; categorical.py 199/202 is exactly that convention, materialized, so the precedence question is not a maintainer call an implementer must go ask about -- the in-repo precedent answers it. What actually remains is that the issue author poses 'Always a good idea? How do we defer to the theme if the user wants to force a grid?' and does not answer it, leaving the forced-grid case as a narrow unstated expected behavior: U2, matching r1. r2's U6 secondary comes from the author calling the invisible-artist/sticky-edges approach a 'hack', but that is implementation mechanics for an already-specified observable outcome (limits pinned at +/-0.5, margin 0), and per calibration patch difficulty is not a decidability blocker, so it does not survive as a secondary either; clarification_target 'convention' falls with U5. r1 is kept as base because at P1/U2 with empty secondary_blockers and null clarification_target it is already consistent with that resolution and needs zero overrides, whereas r2 would need primary_blocker, secondary_blockers, clarification_target and its rationale all rewritten. r2's direction wording is the more granular of the two (it names the exact expected y-limits of (n - 0.5, -0.5)) but it is the same three-element target as r1's, so this is wording, not disagreement, and it is not worth carrying four overrides to obtain.

The two directions are the same three elements -- Value's output-field resolution in django/db/models/expressions.py, triggered by a Value(stdlib literal) with no output_field= argument, observably resolving to an inferred Field instead of raising FieldError -- so only the blocker axis is live. r2's mechanism claims check out line for line: class Value is at expressions.py 677, its __init__(self, value, output_field=None) at 683, and BaseExpression.output_field at 266-273 raises FieldError('Cannot resolve expression type, unknown output_field') at line 272 when _resolve_output_field() returns None; Value defines no _resolve_output_field override, and the ones that exist (Subquery at 1059, Window at 1241) just forward a source expression's field, which Value has none of. The blocker turns on what the packet does and does not fix about the type-to-field mapping. It does not fix it: the only Python-type-to-Field precedent anywhere in the retrieved code is _combine at expressions.py 59-64, which special-cases datetime.timedelta to DurationField() and nothing else; docs/ref/models/expressions.txt documents Value and output_field without listing any inferred mapping; and every visible test spells the field out by hand (tests/expressions/tests.py:487 Value(1, output_field=IntegerField()), :1013 Value(None, output_field=DurationField()), tests/annotations/tests.py:119 and :167 the same pattern), so no visible test encodes an inferred result. Choosing CharField versus TextField for str, or FloatField versus DecimalField for a Decimal, is therefore a Django API convention call that the artifact leaves open -- U5 with clarification_target 'convention', as r2 has it. r1 reached U2 but its own rationale concedes the point, calling the mapping 'a bounded assumption the annotator must fill in conventionally'; the expected behavior itself is not ambiguous (the reporter's update() should compile and run rather than raise), only the conventional mapping is, so U2 mislabels the residual. r2 is base because it already carries U5 plus the matching clarification_target and needs no overrides, and its provenance pins both files at base_commit d08e6f55 while r1's is bare paths.

The code facts both passes lean on verify: SysCaptureBinary.writeorg is src/_pytest/capture.py 644-646 and does 'self._old.write(data); self._old.flush()' where self._old is the saved sys stream captured at line 602 (getattr(sys, name)), while the sibling FDCaptureBinary.writeorg at 571-575 performs the mirror-image conversion ('if isinstance(data, str): data = data.encode("utf8")') before os.write; the flush path r2 names, MultiCapture.pop_outerr_to_orig, is at 429-435 and calls self.out.writeorg(out). So the defect and the direction are the same on both sides -- convert in SysCaptureBinary.writeorg so a binary sys capture can flush back to the original stream -- and the wording difference (r2 also allows writing through the stream's buffer) is two renderings of one observable outcome, not two targets. The live axis is data_quality. r2's Q2 does not survive: category_status reports issue_packet materialized with source_snapshot_verified, so the packet is not mis-assembled; the thin body ('Fixes .../issues/6871') is what the upstream artifact actually says, and linked_artifacts is declared unavailable (edit_history_unavailable) rather than silently dropped, which is the ordinary available-only condition this batch is judged under, not a benchmark packaging mismatch. That gap is already priced in by the U1 both passes agree on, so double-counting it as Q2 would be wrong. I therefore base on r2 and override data_quality to Q0. r2 is the better substrate despite needing that one override: its provenance pins both files at base_commit c26bbdfa, it is the only side that actually consumed visible_tests, its direction cites the exact call chain and failure text, and its clarification_target 'reproduction' matches the shared U1 blocker more precisely than r1's null.

Same behavior target on both sides -- validate the shape of ADMINS/MANAGERS at the top of mail_admins()/mail_managers() and fail immediately instead of building recipients from malformed entries -- so only the blocker axis is live. r2's code citations are exact: mail_admins is django/core/mail/__init__.py line 89 and mail_managers line 104, and each builds recipients with '[a[1] for a in settings.ADMINS]' (line 96) / '[a[1] for a in settings.MANAGERS]' (line 111), which is why a flat list of address strings silently yields single characters as recipients and only fails as the SMTPRecipientsRefused the reporter pasted. What decides U2 versus U5 is that the expected behavior is in fact stated, twice: the issue title is imperative ('Raise exceptions ... when settings are not in expected formats'), the body asks for Django to 'fail early', and the expected format itself is pinned in the packet by django/conf/global_settings.py line 25, whose comment documents ADMINS as "[('Full Name', 'email@example.com'), ('Full Name', 'anotheremail@example.com')]" (with MANAGERS = ADMINS at line 168). So neither the trigger condition nor the desired outcome is ambiguous, which is what U2 would assert. What genuinely floats is which exception class and message Django uses for a bad setting -- and that is not derivable here, because no ImproperlyConfigured or comparable settings-error idiom appears anywhere in the retrieved evidence (grepping mail/__init__.py, global_settings.py and utils/log.py turns up none; the only nearby raises are unrelated, e.g. PermissionDenied in middleware/common.py line 45). Picking among ValueError, ImproperlyConfigured or a checks-framework message is a house-style call, so U5 with clarification_target 'convention' is the right characterisation, as r2 has it; r1's own rationale concedes the residual is 'the exception class and message wording' while still selecting U2. r2 is base with no overrides: it already carries U5 plus the matching clarification_target, its provenance pins the file at base_commit 29240a99, and its direction names both call sites by line and states the current wrong observable rather than only the intended one.

The shared mechanism holds at base_commit c1e4111c, not just in the reporter's Django 3.0.5 traceback: BaseDatabaseSchemaEditor._alter_field is django/db/backends/base/schema.py line 621, and at lines 809-810 it does 'if self._unique_should_be_added(old_field, new_field): self.execute(self._create_unique_sql(model, [new_field]))', while alter_unique_together at 415-429 drops the old composed index via _delete_composed_index (452). With the pasted 0002 sequencing AlterField ahead of AlterUniqueTogether, the add fires while the identically named index still exists, which is exactly the sqlmigrate output the reporter included. Both passes are P1 on the same target, so the decisive check was retrieval_sufficiency and it settles the blocker with it. r2's claim is verifiable and correct: django/db/migrations/autodetector.py -- the module that would have to change under the direction both passes favour -- is not in retrieved_code, which carries operations/fields.py, operations/models.py, executor.py, migration.py and base/schema.py but no autodetector; r1 marked retrieval 'sufficient' and listed tests/migrations/test_autodetector.py in its provenance, but that is the test file, present in visible_tests, not the module. So 'insufficient' plus r2's explicit missing_repository_evidence entry is the accurate reading of the packet. On the blocker itself, the residual is not a house-style question: it is whether the intended outcome is a reordered generated migration or a schema editor taught to tolerate a pre-existing single-column unique index -- two different observable end states, with the issue title ('generate an invalid migration') tilting to the former but never saying so outright. That is unstated expected behavior, U2 with clarification_target 'expected_behavior' as r2 has it, not U5; nothing here turns on knowing a Django convention. The directions agree on all three elements (drop the unique_together index before creating the field-level unique, so migrate completes instead of failing with 1061 Duplicate key name) -- r1 merely hedges the hosting layer with an 'and/or', which is the wording difference flagged on this row, not a second target. Base r2 with no overrides: it already carries U2, the matching clarification_target, the correct retrieval verdict and git-pinned provenance.

The two passes make opposite factual claims about the current behavior and r2's is the correct one. At base_commit b68caad8, IndexedBase.__new__ is sympy/tensor/indexed.py line 380; it pops offset (399) and strides (400) out of kw_args and then calls 'Expr.__new__(cls, label, shape)' (403) or 'Expr.__new__(cls, label)' (405) -- kw_args is never forwarded. So IndexedBase('x', positive=True) does not raise at this commit; the extra keyword is silently dropped, exactly as r2 says. The reporter's pasted traceback ('obj = Expr.__new__(cls, label, **kw_args)') comes from an older build, and the only place that still forwards kwargs is Indexed.__new__ at line 159, which is not the call the reporter made. r1's direction is therefore built on a stale current-state ('no TypeError is raised' as the acceptance surface), which is why I keep r2's direction and provenance rather than r1's. The blocker axis goes the other way. r2's U5 rests on the choice between building the label as an assumption-carrying Symbol and stamping _assumptions directly, but both mechanisms are in the packet and produce the same observable (x.is_positive and x[1].is_positive True, sqrt(x[1]**2) collapsing): Idx already does 'obj._assumptions["finite"] = True' at indexed.py 611-612 -- the precedent the reporter himself links -- and Symbol.__new__(cls, name, **assumptions) with _sanitize is at core/symbol.py 168-202. A choice between two renderings of one observable outcome, with in-repo precedent for both, is not what pins this row. What is genuinely unstated is scope: the reporter asks for IndexedBase outright but marks Indexed.__new__ accepting per-element assumptions as merely 'optionally', so whether that second surface is in the intended behavior is left open. That is U2, as r1 had it, and I set clarification_target to 'expected_behavior' to match; r2's 'convention' and its U2 secondary both fall out with U5. Base is r2 because its direction, its statement of the pre-change observable and its git-pinned provenance survive intact, leaving only the three blocker-side fields to override.

overrides.predicted_direction: Make the enable/disable message-state options that come from a configuration file independent of the line order in which they appear, so a pylintrc containing disable=fixme and enable=all yields every check enabled except fixme whichever line comes first, while leaving command-line ordering semantics untouched.

predicted_direction_template.component_or_function: The config-file application path for message state: _config_initialization in pylint/config/config_initialization.py, which parses the file into config_args (line 42) and applies them in their own pass via linter._parse_configuration_file(config_args) (line 60), driving the enable/disable options declared in pylint/lint/base_options.py lines 183-224 (_EnableAction/_DisableAction) into _MessageStateHandler._set_msg_status in pylint/lint/message_state_handler.py (line 129).
predicted_direction_template.input_condition_or_trigger: A pylintrc [MESSAGES CONTROL] section that combines a broad 'all' entry with specific message ids across the two keys - the reporter's case being disable=fixme on an earlier line than enable=all - with no equivalent flags given on the command line.
predicted_direction_template.observable_behavior_change: That run reports every check except fixme, the same result as swapping the two lines and the same as `pylint --enable=all --disable=fixme`. Today the key that the file lists second wins outright, so enable=all overwrites the earlier disable and fixme messages are still emitted.

resolution_notes: The mechanism both passes describe verifies: pylint/config/config_initialization.py parses the rcfile into config_args (line 42) and applies them in a dedicated pass at line 60 (linter._parse_configuration_file(config_args)), and the enable/disable options at pylint/lint/base_options.py 183-224 are wired through _EnableAction/_DisableAction into _MessageStateHandler._set_msg_status (message_state_handler.py 129), so the key appearing later in the file simply overwrites the earlier one. On the blocker axis r2 is right. The reporter states his wanted outcome without ambiguity ('disable=fixme' + 'enable=all' should mean everything except fixme), so U2 mischaracterises the gap; what is unrecorded is which general precedence rule the project wants, and the packet shows that is a live policy question rather than a lookup. base_options.py lines 215-221 (echoed verbatim in the shipped pylintrc comments at lines 95-99) documents the opposite idiom as the sanctioned one -- '--disable=all --enable=similarities' and '--disable=all --enable=classes --disable=W' -- so any rule chosen has to decide what an rcfile with disable=all plus enable=<specific> now means. That is U5 with clarification_target 'convention'. That same evidence is why I override r2's direction. r2 commits to 'apply enable before disable for file-sourced options', which would invert the documented disable=all/enable=specific idiom, while its own rationale calls that tie-break undetermined - an internally incoherent pairing. r1's rule ('all' before specific) is the other tie-break and preserves the idiom, but it is equally unsupported by the artifacts. I therefore restate the direction at the level the issue actually pins - order-independence for file-sourced message state, with the reporter's exact case as the acceptance surface, CLI semantics untouched - which is coherent with U5. Equivalence is partially_equivalent, not equivalent: the two rules agree on the reported input but diverge observably on an rcfile carrying disable=all with enable=<specific>, which the issue never specifies. The packet corroborates that target directly, because CHANGES already opens with 'Release 4.0.2 (in development)' at L2 and lists under Incompatible changes at L11-13 '#9217: manpage: Stop creating a section directory on build manpage by default (see :confval:`man_make_section_directory`)'. Two things stop this being fully settled. First, the packet's own documentation contradicts itself: doc/usage/configuration.rst L1615-1622 states in prose 'If true, make a section directory on build man page.  Default is True.' while the versionchanged:: 4.0 note immediately below it reads 'The default is changed to ``False`` from ``True``.' - so the confval entry simultaneously asserts both defaults and must itself be corrected by the change. Second, the reporter's separate point that the builder emits '<builddir>/1' rather than '<builddir>/man1', which is the only form MANPATH accepts, is raised as an aside without saying whether it belongs in the same change; tests/test_build_manpage.py L33-37 pins the current opt-in layout as (app.outdir / '1' / 'python.1') under confoverrides={'man_make_section_directory': True}, so flipping that naming would be an observable second change. That scope question is the U2 residual, hence P1. sphinx/builders/manpage.py, which holds the add_config_value call and the path construction, is absent from the retrieval (eleven of the twelve retrieved_code items are locale/*/LC_MESSAGES/sphinx.po catalogues), so retrieval is insufficient even though the issue and the changelog pin the direction.

resolution_notes: Both passes are P1/U2 and give the same behavior target - restore man_make_section_directory to default False so a plain sphinx-build -b man writes pages flat into the output directory, with the manN-vs-N naming of the opt-in layout as the attached open question - so the wording axis is equivalent. Base is r2 because it used docs evidence r1 ignored, and that evidence is what actually anchors the row: CHANGES at the base commit d6c19126c5ebd788619d491d4e70c949de9fd2ff opens 'Release 4.0.2 (in development)' (L58) and already carries, under Incompatible changes, '#9217: manpage: Stop creating a section directory on build manpage by default' (L68-69), while L137-138 records the 4.0 change that introduced the default. r1 reached the same place from the issue text alone and listed only tests/test_build_manpage.py. I kept r2's secondary U4, which I verified is real. SUBSTANTIVE CORRECTION to an earlier version of this note, which had read only the first eight lines of the confval entry and wrongly called r2's description 'backwards': r2 is right and the earlier reading was wrong. The full entry at doc/usage/configuration.rst L2351-2362 gives 'If true, make a section directory on build man page.  Default is True.' (L2353), then '.. versionchanged:: 4.0' / 'The default is changed to ``False`` from ``True``.' (L2356-2358), and then '.. versionchanged:: 4.0.2' / 'The default is changed to ``True`` from ``False`` again.' (L2360-2362) - exactly the 4.0.2 flip-back-to-True note r2 cited. So the confval entry is internally consistent; the real conflict is between it and CHANGES, whose 4.0.2 'in development' Incompatible changes section carries the #9217 entry quoted above saying the section directory stops being created by default, i.e. default False. The changelog and the confval it cross-references state opposite defaults for the same unreleased version, which is the U4 this record carries. Overrode data_quality Q2 -> Q0: as on the sibling row sphinx-doc__sphinx-8284, the absence of sphinx/builders/manpage.py amid eleven locale/*/LC_MESSAGES/sphinx.po catalogues is a BM25 selection miss already recorded as retrieval_sufficiency: insufficient, not a benchmark packaging mismatch - issue_packet is source_snapshot_verified, repository_inventory base_commit_tree_verified, and the docs and visible_tests that decide the row are materialized. Kept r2's clarification_target expected_behavior, which fits the U2 primary (is the '1' -> 'man1' rename in scope) better than r1's null.

Base is r2 because each of its three specific evidence claims verifies against the frozen packet and they are what make the row auditable. (2) test_axes_class_tuple at lib/mpl_toolkits/axes_grid1/tests/test_axes_grid1.py L589-592 does exactly what r2 says: fig = plt.figure(); axes_class = (mpl_toolkits.axes_grid1.mpl_axes.Axes, {}); gr = AxesGrid(fig, 111, nrows_ncols=(1, 1), axes_class=axes_class) - i.e. the only axes_class coverage in the file is the default mpl_axes flavour, so no visible test encodes the wanted behavior for a foreign class. My own read of dates.py shows a second convention surface neither pass mentions: the module docstring carries an '.. autosummary:: :nosignatures:' block at L58-67 listing exactly the same seven helpers as __all__, so 'make these documented' can mean the __all__ tuple, that autosummary list, both, and optionally the reporter's floated 'Miscellaneous date functions' heading. P1 stands on both sides: the target converges, only the presentation convention is assumed.

Chose r2 as base: its clarification_target of 'tradeoff' matches the shared U6 blocker where r1 left it None, and it carries the extra linked PR #2757 pointer. No overrides.

No overrides.

The two rationales make directly conflicting factual claims about the printer, so I grepped it. r1 asserts sympy/printing/mathematica.py is 'visibly lacking any matrix/array _print methods'; that is false. Both passes give the same behavior target: resolve a FilteredRelation's condition while the relation is being added to the query instead of at compile time, so expressions inside the condition register the joins they reference and the generated SQL stops referring to a table that is absent from FROM. r1 says 'at annotation/aliasing time', r2 says 'while the relation is being added' - as r2 itself notes, annotate time versus alias setup is an implementation choice inside one behavior target, not a behavioural fork, so this is wording. The neighbouring resolve_expression at lines 424-429 raising NotImplementedError('FilteredRelation.resolve_expression() is unused.') reinforces that nothing resolves the condition earlier today. So neither direction names a wrong component or condition. Kept r2 as base: it quotes the actual failing annotate() call from the issue including the Coalesce(F('worker'), F('worker_substitutions__worker')) that reaches through a relation the outer query never traverses, and states the acceptance surface as the compiled query containing the workersubstitution join plus a queryset that evaluates - both checkable against the SQL pasted in the issue body. r1 describes the same outcome generically. Both passes target the same observable outcome - a Window/OVER annotation on SQLite older than 3.25.0 fails with django.db.utils.NotSupportedError instead of the sqlite3 driver's OperationalError syntax complaint, via a runtime version gate on supports_over_clause in django/db/backends/sqlite3/features.py - so this is one behavior target, not two. I broke the tie on mechanism accuracy against the frozen code, and here the usual preference for r2 does not hold. r2's rationale asserts that BaseDatabaseOperations.check_expression_support raises NotSupportedError('This backend does not support window expressions.') whenever supports_over_clause is false, and its template names that method as the guard, implying the flag alone is sufficient. The retrieved files say otherwise: base/operations.py l.570-576 defines check_expression_support as a docstring-only stub, sqlite3/operations.py l.43-64 overrides it but only for date/time aggregates and multi-argument DISTINCT aggregates, and the only occurrence of that NotSupportedError message is window_frame_rows_start_end at l.647-648, which is reached solely when a frame is supplied. Window.as_sql does call connection.ops.check_expression_support(self) at expressions.py l.1238-1239, so the hook is invoked, but nothing behind it currently inspects supports_over_clause - a frameless Window would still emit SQL. r1's direction covers exactly that gap by pairing the new feature flag with an explicit NotSupportedError on the Window compilation path. The version-gate idiom r1 relies on is present as claimed (sqlite3/features.py l.25, 36, 40-42 are all Database.sqlite_version_info comparisons). Base r1, no overrides.

Same component (EvaluateFalseTransformer / evaluateFalse in sympy/parsing/sympy_parser.py), same trigger (parse_expr with evaluate=False on a string with Mult or Div inside a function call), same observable change (sqrt(2*2) and sqrt(2/2) come back instead of 2 and 1). Equivalent at behavior level. Their accounts of the mechanism are not equally accurate, though, and that decides the base. sympy_parser.py l.1041-1111 shows EvaluateFalseTransformer defining an operators map, flatten() at l.1053 and visit_BinOp at l.1068, with every constructed ast.Call carrying keywords=[ast.keyword(arg='evaluate', value=NameConstant(False))] - and no ast.Call visitor anywhere in the class. Since NodeTransformer recurses through a call's arguments, the inner 2*2 is already rebuilt as an unevaluated Mul; what is missing is evaluate=False on the sqrt call itself, which is why sqrt collapses the argument while sin does not. r2 states exactly this ('no ast.Call visitor ... a call node's own evaluate keyword is never set'), and the issue body corroborates it directly: the reporter shows sympy.sqrt(sympy.Mul(2,2, evaluate=False), evaluate=False) returning sqrt(2*2) and parse_expr("sqrt(2*2, evaluate=False)", evaluate=False) working, i.e. the functions honour the keyword when it reaches them. r1's phrasing - that arguments under a Call must 'also be kept unevaluated' - misdescribes that internal mechanism, though it names the right component, trigger and outputs, so it is not a wrong-component error and no override applies. Base r2, which also records the acceptance surface completely by listing the sin(2/2), sin(2*2), sin(2+2) and sqrt(2+2) cases that must not regress.

One behavior target on both sides: Pow._eval_subs in sympy/core/power.py must stop deriving a fractional-power match in the noncommutative case, so (x*x*x).subs({x*x: 1}) with x = Symbol('x', commutative=False) returns x rather than 1. So both passes point at real code with the property claimed. One precision difference worth recording: r1 says the guard applies to noncommutative *bases*, while the issue's own diff and r2 both key on the pattern being substituted (not old.is_commutative). In the repro these coincide, and r1 still names the correct function and observable outcome, so it is not a wrong-condition error and no override is needed. Base r2 for the exact guard predicate and for stating the commutative case that must keep working, which is what makes the P0 acceptance surface checkable.

Same behavior target: the docstring lookup sphinx.util.inspect.getdoc performs for autodoc must resolve the inherited docstring when the subclass attribute is a decorator wrapper with no __doc__ of its own, so autoclass renders 'Do stuff.' under MyClass.my_method instead of an empty body. One target on both sides: sympy.core.symbol.symbols must pass the caller's cls down its non-string-container recursion, so symbols(('q:2','u:2'), cls=Function) produces UndefinedFunction instances instead of Symbols. Both passes describe the same observable target - evalf with a subs dictionary on an expression containing floor/ceiling must return the full-precision value, so srepr((floor(x)+20).evalf(subs={x:0.5})) reads Float('20.0', precision=53) and agrees with (floor(x)+20).subs({x:0.5}).evalf(), instead of Float('16.0', precision=1) - and both explicitly note that the two candidate mechanisms (substitute before the integer-part helper, or make that helper report honest accuracy) collapse to the same result. This one is not a wording split. The issue body enumerates three changes: (1) nullable m2m AND fk relations return an empty queryset when the relation field is null - previously an error for m2m, no change for fk; (2) adding to a fk relation with a null relation field becomes an error; (3) using any relation on an unsaved object becomes an error. r1 reproduces all three. r2 instead directs that the reverse fk manager refuse to query 'when the owning instance has no primary key OR a null join value', and its rationale asserts bullet one is already satisfied. The frozen code shows that reading is wrong on both halves. related_descriptors.py:650-653 has _apply_rel_filters returning queryset.none() when a foreign_related_fields value is None - so bullet one's fk half is indeed already satisfied, but r2's direction would replace that none() with a raise, which is the opposite of what bullet one asks for fk. And the m2m half is not satisfied: the ManyRelatedManager constructor still raises ValueError at lines 955-960 when None is in related_val, exactly the error bullet one wants relaxed to an empty queryset (the separate unsaved-pk raise at 964-969 is bullet three's model, not bullet one's). So r2 both inverts one stated condition and drops a required behavior change, leaving only bullet three shared. Base r1, which tracks the issue's bullets verbatim; P1/U6 stands unchanged since the tradeoff the reporter flags is the backwards-compat cost, so no overrides.
